title: Knowledge Check 4: Lessons 25-32
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 25-32 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Before building, a team decides the whole user-facing operation may take a fixed total time and gives each step its own slice. What does that decision buy them?
options: It gives every step an equal share of the total time, no matter how much work that step does.
It splits one total time target into per-step slices, so the step that overruns is obvious.
It guarantees the operation meets its target without measuring any step.
It removes the need to cache or batch any repeated work.
questions.explanation: A budget makes the slow step visible, because the one that exceeds its allocation is the one to fix rather than an unnamed accumulation.

questions.question: An interactive turn must stay fast while a bulk path handles high volume. How should throughput and latency be treated?
options: Maximize throughput first, then check whether latency still meets the target.
Treat them as one axis, since improving either one always improves the other.
Pick a latency target, then push throughput up without breaking it.
Set them independently, because they never trade off against each other.
questions.explanation: Latency and throughput are separate axes that trade against each other, so the right move is to fix a latency target and then raise throughput as high as it can go within that target.

questions.question: When does batching hurt more than it helps?
options: When an interactive user's result would be delayed to fill a larger batch.
When many independent requests can share the same expensive compute step.
When a nightly job enriches a large batch that nobody is actively waiting on.
When requests arrive together and can each tolerate a small wait.
questions.explanation: Batching is a throughput tool with a latency cost, so it is wrong when one waiting user is made to pay that cost to enlarge the batch.

questions.question: Why is walking a large result set with the server's next-page pointer safer than requesting a numbered range of rows?
options: The pointer returns the entire result set in one response, so no loop is required.
The pointer lets a client page through results without ever checking whether more rows remain.
The pointer stays stable when rows are added or removed mid-walk, unlike a numbered range.
The pointer always needs fewer API calls than requesting a numbered range.
questions.explanation: A cursor tracks a fixed position on the server, so inserts or deletes behind the scenes do not shift the set out from under the client the way a numbered offset does.

questions.question: A nightly job must sync tens of thousands of records, while an on-screen action creates one record and needs its ID back at once. Which approach fits each?
options: A bulk ingest job for the nightly sync and a single synchronous call for the on-screen create.
A single synchronous call for both, looped over every record for the nightly sync.
A bulk ingest job for both, since asynchronous always beats synchronous.
A batched synchronous call for the nightly sync and a bulk job for the single on-screen create.
questions.explanation: Match the tool to the latency the work actually needs: high-volume scheduled writes go async in bulk, while an interactive action that needs an immediate answer stays on a single synchronous call.

questions.question: Why does pinning an API version in the request path not remove the need for maintenance?
options: Because the version in the path is ignored once a newer release ships.
Because each pinned version supports only one consumer at a time.
Because pinned versions are retired on a schedule, so pinning schedules the upgrade.
Because pinning forces every consumer of the org onto the newest version the moment it releases.
questions.explanation: A pinned version holds its behavior steady, but the platform retires old versions on a schedule, so pinning schedules the upgrade instead of eliminating it.

questions.question: Why does reaching for a named credential reduce the risk that a secret leaks into source control?
options: It encrypts every callout payload so the secret stays unreadable in transit.
It keeps the endpoint and authentication in setup, so code never holds the secret.
It rotates the stored secret automatically on a fixed nightly schedule.
It blocks every call that does not originate from a trusted address inside the org.
questions.explanation: When the endpoint and the credential live in setup and the code calls the credential by name, there is no secret string for anyone to paste into code and commit.

questions.question: In a machine-to-machine flow that authenticates with a signed token and no interactive login, what must the calling system do on every exchange?
options: Mint a fresh token and exchange it each time, holding the private key.
Request a refresh token once and reuse it until it expires.
Sign the token with a password stored in the connected app.
Let the authorization server generate and rotate the signing key on demand.
questions.explanation: No interactive login means no refresh token, so the caller keeps the signing key and re-mints a new signed token on each exchange, which makes expiration and clock accuracy its own responsibility.

questions.question: What question does IP allowlisting answer, and how does it relate to strong authentication?
options: It proves the caller's identity cryptographically and can replace token validation entirely.
It encrypts all traffic in transit, so separate authentication tokens become unnecessary.
It restricts which network ranges may reach the app, a layer on top of strong auth.
It verifies the caller's certificate chain each time during the connection handshake.
questions.explanation: Allowlisting answers a cruder, earlier question, whether the caller is even from a recognized place, so it is defense in depth and not a replacement for proving identity.

questions.question: A streaming subscriber disconnects for a few hours. Why can it catch up later without losing the events it missed?
options: The bus retains messages for a fixed window, so the subscriber resumes from its last position.
The producer keeps republishing every single message until each subscriber acknowledges that it received it.
The subscriber polls the bus for any missed events once it has reconnected successfully.
Delivery is guaranteed only to subscribers that stay connected the whole time.
questions.explanation: Messages persist in the bus for a bounded retention window, so a subscriber that saved its position replays from there and closes the gap left by the disconnect.

questions.question: A consumer relies on the order in which events published through separate publish calls arrive. What is true about that order?
options: Order is guaranteed across calls because the platform routes each org through one server.
Order is guaranteed within a single publish call but not across separate calls.
Order is never guaranteed, even within a single publish call.
Order is guaranteed only for change-data events, not for platform events.
questions.explanation: Events in one publish call keep their passed order, but separate requests can be handled by different servers at different speeds, so cross-call order is not something to depend on.

questions.question: An org with a fixed daily delivery allocation streams the same events to two external subscribers. How is its usage counted?
options: Once per message, since delivery counts the event and not the subscriber.
Only for subscribers that sit outside the org, and only for platform events.
Per subscriber, so two subscribers draw the same shared pool twice over.
Not at all, because the delivery allocation does not apply to streaming subscribers.
questions.explanation: Delivery usage is counted for each subscribed client and added across subscribers, so adding a consumer is a second charge against the same pool rather than a free read.

questions.question: Why must a test that exercises an external callout register a mock rather than reach the live service?
options: Because real callouts are slow to run but still reach the live external service during a test run.
Because no real network calls happen in test context, so a mock supplies the response.
Because the external vendor blocks every request that comes from a test run.
Because callout logic cannot be covered by any automated test.
questions.explanation: The platform refuses the network call while a test runs, so the mock is how the test states what the external system would have returned and pins down how the code should react.

questions.question: Which sandbox type is the one that supports performance and load testing of an integration path?
options: A Developer sandbox, because it refreshes the fastest.
A Developer Pro sandbox, because it raises the data allowance.
A Partial Copy sandbox, because it copies a template-defined subset of records.
A Full sandbox, because it is a complete replica of production.
questions.explanation: Load and performance testing need the whole org, and the full replica is the only sandbox type where that level of testing is supported.

questions.question: What does wrapping the exercised code in the start-test and stop-test calls give a test?
options: A fresh set of governor limits and synchronous execution of queued async work.
A rollback of every DML operation so that the org data is left completely untouched.
A way to run the test without registering a callout mock first.
An automatic retry of any assertion that fails the first time.
questions.explanation: The wrapped section runs under its own limit budget, and queued async work is flushed synchronously at the stop call so the test can assert on the result without waiting.

questions.question: How do capability checks and regression checks differ in what they expect and what they are for?
options: Capability checks start at a low pass rate; regression checks stay near complete.
Capability checks stay near complete, while regression checks deliberately start at a low pass rate.
Both kinds start low and both are expected to climb toward completion.
Both kinds stay near complete, since both confirm behavior that already works.
questions.explanation: A capability check is a hill to climb that starts low, while a regression check is a safety net held near complete, so a drop on the capability suite cannot answer whether something broke.

questions.question: What makes a golden set trustworthy as the anchor for regression runs?
options: It holds only hand-written happy-path examples that the system already passes.
It is built once and frozen so the baseline never moves again.
It mirrors production traffic, including edge and adversarial cases.
It scores model outputs with fluency measures such as perplexity and BLEU.
questions.explanation: A set that does not reproduce real traffic is a biased design, and because production keeps changing the set has to be grown and refreshed to stay a faithful reference.

questions.question: Why is watching only error rate and latency not enough when canarying a new model version?
options: Because error rate and latency cannot be measured on live production traffic.
Because a model can be technically healthy yet produce worse reasoning, tone, or accuracy.
Because canaries apply only to infrastructure changes and not to models.
Because output variability makes error rate and latency the only dependable signals to watch.
questions.explanation: Infrastructure dashboards can look clean while output quality quietly slips, so hallucination, coherence, judge, and business signals belong in the canary from the first stage.

questions.question: A business operation must be callable from a UI, a batch job, and an API, and the object's calculation rules should be shared by all three callers. Where does each piece belong?
options: The service layer exposes the operation and the object's domain class holds the calculation.
The trigger owns the operation, because it runs for every record change on the object.
The selector class owns the operation, because it already queries the object for the caller.
Each entry point implements the rule for itself, so the logic stays close to the caller that needs it.
questions.explanation: The service layer is the process entry point every caller shares, and object behavior belongs in the domain class so the trigger and the service cannot disagree.

questions.question: Why is a trigger a poor home for nontrivial business logic?
options: Because a trigger is invoked for a single record at a time, so it cannot handle a whole collection.
Because a trigger cannot be called from other entry points, so its logic gets copied and drifts.
Because the platform forbids queries inside a trigger body.
Because trigger logic cannot be tested or deployed with changesets.
questions.explanation: A trigger is not a reusable class, so logic placed there cannot be shared with other entry points and ends up duplicated and inconsistent across them.

questions.question: A bulk load inserts thousands of records and the object's logic queries once per record. What does the selector pattern change?
options: It moves the query into the trigger so it runs once per transaction.
It removes the need to bulkify because the selector caches each record it loads.
It centralizes the query behind set-based criteria for the whole collection.
It splits the large load into single-record transactions so each one stays under the limits.
questions.explanation: Triggers run in bulk, so a query per record spends the shared budget in proportion to load size; a selector that takes a collection and queries once keeps the logic bulk safe.

questions.question: A process must coordinate Salesforce with an external planning system and a separate warehouse system, each with a different payload. Where does the orchestration belong?
options: In a record-triggered flow on the Salesforce object, so that the whole handoff stays inside the org itself.
In an Apex trigger, because only Apex can call out to an external system.
In the external layer, with Salesforce publishing an event and the coordinator driving the rest.
In a scheduled flow that polls the other systems on a fixed recurring interval.
questions.explanation: Orchestration across systems that Salesforce does not own belongs in the layer that owns them, so the platform publishes the business event and lets the external layer coordinate the rest.

questions.question: A finance process must commit its work or roll the whole change back if a boundary check fails. Which home fits and why?
options: Flow, because it offers a built-in rollback step for this case.
Apex, because Flow has no savepoint or rollback for partial-commit control.
Either one, because Flow and Apex express transaction control equally well.
External automation, because transaction control is a cross-system concern.
questions.explanation: Savepoint, rollback, and partial commit are capabilities Flow does not expose, so a transactional-control requirement is an Apex requirement rather than a Flow shortcoming to work around.

questions.question: An object carries fifteen to thirty automations, moderate batch volumes, coupled parent and child updates, and some recursion risk. Which standard fits?
options: A hybrid: keep the record-triggered flow as the entry point and move the compute into invocable Apex.
One very large record-triggered flow that handles every single rule the team could think of on that object.
A full migration to an Apex trigger behind a metadata framework.
External automation, since any risk of recursion is really a cross-system problem.
questions.explanation: Medium density is the hybrid case: the flow keeps one readable, ordered entry point while the compute Flow handles poorly moves behind an invocable Apex seam.
